en: All the guards were thrown into turmoil,
And his true courage was revealed.
Some champions could not endure it,
And their appointed death overtook them.
They ride steeds swift as bullets,
And every one bears a steel spear.
They wear black hats as broad as cauldrons,
And look like angels of death.
No mortal dares approach them,
Yet they do not torment the world without cause.
But any mortal who provokes them
Does not escape death alive.”
The prudent maiden Külayim,
Her envoy at her side,
Who lived and rose together with her
And devised wise counsel for her,
Her most trusted attendant,
The strongest in finding a way,
Upon hearing this news,
Sprang up and darted like a doe,
Showing her graceful skill,
And, fairest of all with arched dark brows,
Now began to speak words of joy.
To the forlorn maiden sitting silently,
She joyfully announced:
“Your handsome lion has arrived;
Say no more—God has granted him to you.
His figure is as vast as half a mountain;
Your destined partner has arrived.
More awe-inspiring than other men,
Your lion has arrived.
The traveler has journeyed the road,
And what you lacked has come into your hands.
Blessing has come to your feast;
Your valiant one is now within your grasp.
Your falcon has been caught in the snare;
Your precious lion has been found.
You used to hang your life
By a single thread, dear sister.
The man promised to you has come,
And God has opened the way to your fortune;
May He bless your husband!
A champion came bearing the news
And eagerly began his tale.
Your gold-adorned throne
He simply trampled beneath his feet.
He is the very image of the magnanimous hero;
He is unmistakably Seytek himself.
Look, God has granted your wish;
The lion you desired has arrived.
Riding twin thoroughbred steeds,
They have traveled the road steadfastly.
Your sheltering poplar is now within your grasp;
Speak, sister, and answer me.
As for those heroes who have come,
From what I saw, they are of this kind:
They could sweep aside eighty-four
Mountains of armor, leaving crimson fire behind.
Their presence is supreme, their wrath is strong;
They level whatever lies before them.
He is tall and broad-shouldered,
Both a champion and a lion,
And seems beyond compare.
His heroism is unlike any other;
His figure appeared as vast as a mountain.
Unable to endure his fury,
The watchmen and guards scattered.
No man could remain and look upon him;
They despaired of their lives.
His courage is lofty as a mountain ridge,
As though he would devour anyone who fought him.
His build is like a towering haze,
His stature like a plane tree,
His keenness like a hunting falcon’s.
No living soul can endure his presence;
No mortal can stand before him—
Such is his heroism.
He rides a peerless thoroughbred,
And wears armor no bullet can pierce.
The lion is lofty, his wrath is mighty;
No living soul can equal his bearing—
A lion among men has come.
No man can stand and face him;
Unable to endure his fury,
Many champions were ready to flee.
He bears a tasseled banner,
And all who see his figure rejoice;
His equipment includes a steel spear.
If he grows angry and surges forth,
He could ravage the whole world,
And the hard black earth beneath him
Would tremble to its depths.
No man can contend with him,
No man can defeat him in combat.
Such is his lionheartedness;
No other man is born his equal.
For one who has suffered such distress,
No such lion could be found elsewhere.
He is a handsome, gray-maned lion,
Both a hero and a fierce warrior.
Driven by the fire of love,
He has been searching for you.”
“God has granted your heart’s desire;
The man you wished for has arrived.
God has fulfilled your prayer;
The man you longed for has come.”
Thus Külayim
Joyfully brought her the news.
Then your dear sister Bermet
Spoke softly yet with firm resolve,
Beginning all manner of words,
Thrilled and overcome with haste.
In red and green silk,
She dressed in garments precious as life,
And hung upon her breast
A solid-gold amulet,
Then prayed to the Creator:
“You were my companion, Külayim!
My lady, precious as the Night of Power,
You have rekindled my extinguished fire,
Restored a dead soul to life,
And joined what had been severed.
While Akjoltoy traveled the road without rest,
I plainly withered in misery.
Wearing sores upon every steed,
And grievously tormenting my heart,
I suffered the torments
Of this world and wasted away.
If these words of yours are true,
Then today, Külayim, I rejoice.
My burning heart has been soothed,
And my surging spirit has opened.
The plane tree planted for me has come;
The joyful time for play has come.
A new prosperity has arrived,
And a day of radiant sunlight has dawned.
For tireless play and laughter,
A dark night has fallen upon misfortune,
And news beyond all finding has come.
You tireless beauties,
Every one of you, make haste!
You forlorn maidens who sat in silence,
Put on the garments of the fairies!
You poor dears who walk beside me,
You beauties lovely as paradise,
Whose like cannot be found in this false world,
Whom I cherish more dearly than my life,
It seems to be lion Seytek himself;
All of you, heed my words.”
When the maidens heard this,
In red gowns, with moon-slender waists,
Those graceful darlings,
Upon hearing Bermet’s words,
Could hardly remain without preparing.
When she gave her stately command,
How could the maidens hold back?
The one whose speech was sweet,
The lovely one with gazelle eyes,
The most gifted and graceful of all—
With graceful Külayim at their head—
Put on silk gowns
Fastened with diamond buttons.
By thoughtful observation she could discern
The secrets of the human heart.
Her beauty was perfect,
Setting hearts aflutter anew;
The Creator had made such a mortal.
Everyone who saw her lost his heart;
Her words were sugar and her tongue was honey.
Having taken so fair a maiden,
So kind-hearted a companion,
The ill-fated woman had made ready.
Through the many wonders she displayed,
And the way her beauty stole every beholder’s heart,
Her manner delighted the soul,
And she served her faithfully.
Her beauty was renowned among the people.
Peacock feathers
Were set directly above her crown
In ninety different patterns.
Everyone who looked upon her
Marveled and lost his heart.

Red tea dress

Such was Akbermet's condition.—
That lovely one above all women,
See the snow and see the flesh,
See the blood, and see her face.
Look at the pearls, look at their stitching.
Look at the perfume, smell its fragrance.
Look at her sleeve, look at her hand,
Look at her form, look at her back,
Look at the parrot, see its feathers!
Look at the komuz, hear its sound!
Cock-necked and sheep-eyed,
See the figure of blooming Bermet!
Hear words sweeter than honey,
See Cholpon, look at her eyes.
Her forehead shone like a lamp,
Look at the tall, lovely one herself!
Her waist a handful, her face like the moon,
A famous beauty, that lovely one.
